text:
BERT4Rec reconstructs randomly masked items with bidirectional context but predicts the next item using an appended mask. This creates a plausible supervision mismatch, not evidence that the objectives conflict. Petrov and Macdonald’s [RSS study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643), also appearing in an expanded 2025 publication, explicitly discusses this weak correspondence. No located study establishes that a 0.5 reconstruction/terminal mixture causes gradient conflict in this benchmark. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) remains the architectural reference.

[PCGrad](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06782) motivates measuring negative gradient inner products; [GradNorm](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02257) motivates checking gradient magnitudes separately from loss weights. Proposed diagnostic: at the same checkpoint, compute reconstruction and terminal-loss gradients separately for embeddings, each encoder layer, and the output head. Report cosine similarity, both norms, norm ratio, negative-cosine frequency, and zero-gradient cases across paired minibatches. A 0.5 coefficient does not ensure equal influence. Match prefix/example frequency and supervised-target counts; explicitly compare per-target versus per-sequence mean reductions. Disable dropout or pair its randomness to reduce measurement noise.

For a functional probe, temporarily perturb one encoder layer at a time along each objective’s negative gradient, using equal parameter-step norms and restoring the checkpoint afterward. Measure terminal-target loss, rank, margin, and top-10 membership changes on separate training prefixes with fixed candidates. Hide the terminal target completely, append the reserved mask, and read its final nonpadding position. This proposed probe tests local transfer within one BERT4Rec model; gradient agreement alone cannot establish validation gains. Keep model selection tied to the host’s macro validation HR@10.
